note: Head-to-head and alternatives pages. The first five pairs were chosen from US search demand (treg keyword data, 2026-10-29): e2b, daytona, modal, vercel sandbox and cloudflare sandbox are the provider names people search for. InstaBox vs Lizard is an editorial pick (2026-11-12): two Firecracker providers at almost the same price that suit different jobs. Edges are our reading of the sourced feature rows, written by hand per pair.

isolation.why: Same Firecracker isolation and root on both, but only InstaBox documents Docker inside the machine.

sizes-regions.why: InstaBox goes to 32 vCPU and has L4 GPUs; Lizard stops at 8 vCPU but lets you pick US East or EU West.

lifecycle.why: Both pause with memory, but a stopped InstaBox machine keeps its disk, while a stopped Lizard sandbox is deleted.

snapshots-forks.why: Lizard snapshots and forks keep memory and running programs, up to 100 copies; InstaBox copies files only, up to 5.

storage.why: InstaBox includes 200 GiB of disk on Pro and keeps it on stop; Lizard keeps only a 1–50 GB volume on one node.

idle-timers.why: InstaBox pauses an idle machine by itself; Lizard has no idle timer and bills idle time until you pause or kill it.

reaching-it.why: InstaBox has public or private links, real SSH and a raw TCP preview; Lizard has private links only and no SSH protocol.

custom-domains.why: Neither puts your domain on a sandbox link, but Lizard supports custom domains for apps you deploy on it.

outbound-network.why: Lizard includes 2 TB per 30 days at no per-GB charge; InstaBox Pro includes 1 TiB and caps sending at about 50 Mbit/s.

keys-secrets.why: InstaBox can keep the real key outside the machine behind a placeholder; Lizard passes keys as variables any code can read.

ways-to-drive.why: Both have a dashboard, REST, TypeScript and Python SDKs, a CLI and a hosted MCP server; InstaBox adds real SSH.

built-in-agents.why: Both ship Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode (Lizard as one template each) and prompt them from the CLI; neither has a prompt API.

teams-accounts.why: InstaBox has a hard spend cap that stops machines; Lizard says there is no spending cap at all.

billing-models.why: Mirror-image plans ($20 vs $19) that come back as usage; Lizard is about 5% cheaper per hour, InstaBox stops billing when idle.

trials-free-tiers.why: InstaBox has a free machine that never expires; Lizard has a 7-day, $5 trial that needs a card.

company.why: InstaBox has a status page and a SOC 2 Type II report on request; Lizard lists SOC 2 as coming soon but offers a signed DPA.

isolation.why: Both run a Firecracker microVM with its own kernel; Vercel gives root and Docker by default, while E2B documents Docker but starts as a non-root user.

sizes-regions.why: Vercel goes to 32 vCPU in 19 regions; E2B stops at 8 vCPU and 8 GiB self-serve in five regions.

lifecycle.why: E2B pauses with memory, so programs resume where they were; Vercel saves files only and starts a new session.

snapshots-forks.why: E2B snapshots memory and disk without stopping the source and forks up to 20 copies; a manual Vercel snapshot stops the session and keeps files only.

storage.why: Vercel gives 64 GB of disk plus drives that outlive a sandbox; E2B includes 10–20 GiB, and its volumes are a private beta.

idle-timers.why: Both default to five minutes and allow 24 hours on Pro, but E2B can pause with memory instead of ending the session.

reaching-it.why: In new E2B projects, links are private with a token, and SSH runs through a proxy; Vercel exposes up to 15 web ports and a browser terminal but no SSH.

custom-domains.why: Neither has a native custom domain, but E2B documents a proxy setup; Vercel publishes no path for a sandbox port.

outbound-network.why: E2B has open outbound with allow and deny rules but no static IP at any price; Vercel charges $0.15/GB and offers fixed IPs only on Enterprise.

keys-secrets.why: Both keep the real key outside the machine and add it to outbound requests.

ways-to-drive.why: E2B has SSH and a desktop SDK; Vercel has a REST API and a management MCP server. Neither creates a sandbox from the dashboard.

built-in-agents.why: Vercel puts coding agents in its default image; E2B has ten agent templates, none of them the default. Neither has a prompt API.

teams-accounts.why: Vercel has spend management that can pause projects, an activity log and paid SAML; E2B has per-project spending limits but no audit log.

billing-models.why: Vercel bills only active CPU, so waiting is cheap; E2B bills every allocated vCPU at a lower rate, plus $150 a month for Pro.

trials-free-tiers.why: E2B gives a $100 credit with no card; Vercel Hobby is non-commercial and its Pro trial lasts 14 days with $20.

company.why: Vercel is a large, well-funded company with platform-wide SOC 2 and ISO 27001; E2B is a young startup with its own SOC 2 Type II. Neither has a sandbox SLA below Enterprise.

isolation.why: Both run a Firecracker microVM with its own kernel; Cloudflare runs every process as root, while E2B starts as a non-root user.

sizes-regions.why: E2B goes to 8 vCPU and lets you pick one of five regions; Cloudflare stops at 4 vCPU but allows 12 GiB and chooses the location itself.

lifecycle.why: E2B pauses with memory and keeps the disk; Cloudflare has no pause, and stopping wipes the disk.

snapshots-forks.why: E2B snapshots memory and forks a running machine; Cloudflare snapshots files only, kept for 30 days.

storage.why: E2B keeps the disk through pause and snapshots; Cloudflare wipes its 20 GB disk on stop but can back up to R2 or mount a bucket that outlives every instance.

idle-timers.why: E2B can pause an idle sandbox and allows 24 hours on Pro; Cloudflare has no default timeout, a 6-hour maximum and no pause.

reaching-it.why: New E2B projects get token-protected links by default, plus SSH through a proxy; Cloudflare reaches a sandbox only through your own Worker, with no built-in login.

custom-domains.why: Cloudflare routes your domain to sandbox previews through a Worker and DNS on its own network; E2B needs a proxy server you run yourself.

outbound-network.why: E2B is open by default with allow and deny rules; Cloudflare starts closed and, with the internet off, reaches only HTTP and HTTPS hosts you intercept. It includes 1 TB a month in North America and Europe.

keys-secrets.why: Both add the real key to outbound requests outside the machine, so code inside never sees it.

ways-to-drive.why: E2B has Python and JavaScript SDKs, a CLI and SSH; Cloudflare is driven only from TypeScript inside your Worker.

built-in-agents.why: E2B has ten ready-made agent templates; Cloudflare has guides and an experimental harness for Claude Code or Codex. Neither has a prompt API.

teams-accounts.why: E2B sets a spending limit per project; Cloudflare budget alerts only warn and cannot stop usage.

billing-models.why: Cloudflare bills only active CPU, charges about half E2B's rate for memory, and its plan is $5 a month; E2B bills every allocated vCPU, and Pro is $150.

trials-free-tiers.why: E2B gives a $100 credit with no card; Cloudflare has no free tier and needs the $5 Workers Paid plan.

company.why: Cloudflare is a large public company with company-wide certificates that do not name Sandboxes; E2B is a young startup whose SOC 2 Type II covers its own service. Neither publishes a sandbox SLA.

isolation.why: E2B runs every sandbox as a Firecracker microVM; Modal defaults to gVisor and offers a VM only on request, and its GPU sandboxes are gVisor-only.

sizes-regions.why: Modal sizes CPU and memory freely, offers up to 8 GPUs and lets you pick a region at a surcharge; E2B stops at 8 vCPU and 8 GiB self-serve with no GPU.

lifecycle.why: E2B pauses with memory and resumes the same sandbox; Modal has no pause, only terminate and restore a copy from a snapshot.

snapshots-forks.why: E2B snapshots memory without stopping the source and forks up to 20 live copies; a Modal memory snapshot ends the source and lasts seven days.

storage.why: Modal gives a fixed 512 GiB disk plus volumes that outlive a sandbox; E2B includes 10–20 GiB, and its volumes are a private beta.

idle-timers.why: Both default to five minutes and cap at 24 hours, but E2B can pause an idle sandbox while Modal only terminates it.

reaching-it.why: New E2B projects get token-protected links and SSH through a proxy; Modal tunnels can expose raw TCP and use connect tokens for HTTP, but have no SSH.

custom-domains.why: Modal attaches your domain to sandbox tunnels on Team plans; E2B needs a proxy server you run yourself.

outbound-network.why: E2B has no egress charge but no static IP at any price; Modal charges $0.04/GiB past a large allowance and sells static IPs on Team.

keys-secrets.why: E2B keeps keys outside the sandbox with a proxy by default; Modal passes them in as environment variables unless you use its beta outbound policy.

ways-to-drive.why: E2B has Python and JavaScript SDKs, a CLI and SSH; Modal has Python, JavaScript and Go SDKs and a CLI but no SSH, REST API or management MCP server.

built-in-agents.why: E2B has ten ready-made agent templates; Modal ships no agent, and its browser and desktop are a documented Computer Use example (Chromium over VNC) you build and run yourself, not a ready template.

teams-accounts.why: Modal has workspace and environment budgets that stop spending, roles and service users on Team; E2B has per-project limits but every member has the same permissions.

billing-models.why: Both bill allocated resources per second, but E2B charges about $0.05 a vCPU-hour and $0.016 a GiB-hour against Modal's $0.07 and $0.024.

trials-free-tiers.why: E2B gives $100 once with no card; Modal gives $30 every month but needs a payment method.

company.why: Modal is a large, well-funded company with a SOC 2 Type II report; E2B is a younger startup with its own SOC 2 Type II. Neither publishes an SLA below Enterprise.
